subject: Accounting
title: Theranos: Not Quite Accounting
description: A short lesson to help you apply Theranos: Not Quite Accounting.

hook.text: Theranos wasn't a classic accounting fraud—but it shows how fake numbers destroy trust.

buildup.text: Elizabeth Holmes claimed her device could run 200 blood tests from a single finger prick.

discovery.text: Revenue projections and technology claims were wildly fabricated to attract investors.

twist.text: The company secretly ran most tests on competitors' machines while lying about its own.

climax.text: Holmes was convicted of fraud and sentenced to over 11 years in prison.

punchline.text: When the numbers are fantasy, the story always ends.

quiz.question: What was Theranos accused of?
options: Fabricating technology claims and financial projections

details.summary: While not a traditional accounting fraud, Theranos deceived investors about the capabilities of its blood-testing technology, raising $700 million on false claims. This topic explores why Theranos is studied alongside accounting scandals and what it teaches about due diligence.
details.whyItMatters: Theranos extends the definition of financial fraud beyond accounting manipulation. Misrepresenting your product to raise capital is a form of securities fraud with identical consequences for investors.
takeaways: Theranos claimed its Edison device could run hundreds of tests from a single drop of blood—it couldn't
The company was valued at $9 billion before collapsing to zero when the deception was exposed
Founder Elizabeth Holmes was convicted of investor fraud and sentenced to over 11 years in prison

faq.question: What was the Theranos fraud?
faq.answer: Theranos was primarily a technology fraud — the blood-testing devices never worked as claimed. But it shares DNA with accounting scandals: inflated revenue, misleading investors, suppressed internal dissent, and a board that failed to provide oversight or demand verification.

faq.question: How was the Theranos fraud exposed?
faq.answer: Wall Street Journal reporter John Carreyrou published a series of investigative articles based on whistleblower tips from former employees, revealing that Theranos's technology didn't work as claimed. The company collapsed and Holmes was convicted of fraud.
